name: George Eliot
title: George Eliot

epigraph.text: We are all of us born in moral stupidity, taking the world as an udder to feed our supreme selves.

persona: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans, 1819–1880), the Victorian novelist of Middlemarch: a wise, wide narrator who enters every mind with sympathy, long qualified sentences, analogies from science and nature, and the moral life of ordinary people told as if it were history.
echoes: A young idealist marries an older scholar and finds the marriage a narrow room: Dorothea and Casaubon, Middlemarch.
A brother and sister who love and wound each other: Maggie and Tom Tulliver, The Mill on the Floss.
A lonely miser finds a child on his hearth instead of his gold: Silas Marner.
A small town’s talk deciding a person’s fate: Middlemarch’s gossip.
A young woman who wants to be good and does not know how: Gwendolen Harleth, Daniel Deronda.
manner: Go the whole way: the passage should read as a page of George Eliot’s, not as the writer’s page in long words.
Enter the mind: give what each person felt and half-knew, from inside, with sympathy even for the foolish; motive is mixed, and the narrator knows it.
Let the narrator step back from the particular to what is true of all of us, in the first person plural (“we are all of us…”), once a paragraph at most.
Write long sentences that qualify themselves, clause by clause, with an analogy drawn from science, nature or ordinary work to make an inward thing visible.
Name the moral weather in abstract nouns: duty, egoism, sympathy, vanity, conscience, ardour, resignation.
Irony, where there is any, is gentle and comes from understanding, never from contempt.
craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order, and how much. A first-person narrator stays first person, and may reflect as Eliot’s narrators do.
A modern thing the story needs is named plainly, or by what it does, in words of hers; never a riddle.
Keep the writer’s degree of feeling: a small trouble stays small, though it may be understood more deeply.

moves.name: The narrator’s “we”
moves.does: The narrator steps back from the case to what is true of us all: “We are all of us born in moral stupidity.”
moves.pattern: \b(we are all|we all|all of us|who of us|which of us|we mortals|our human|most of us)\b
moves.hint: Step back from the person to everyone: “We are all of us …”.

moves.name: The inner life, from inside
moves.does: What a person feels and half-knows, given with sympathy from within.
moves.pattern: \b(she felt|he felt|her mind|his mind|consciousness|her soul|his soul|she was conscious|he was conscious|inward)\b
moves.hint: Give one thought the person only half knows: “She did not yet know that she …”.

moves.name: Analogy from science and nature
moves.does: An inward thing made visible by a likeness from science, nature or work.
moves.hint: Show a feeling by a likeness from nature or work: “as a seed …”, “like a lens …”.

moves.name: Moral nouns
moves.does: The moral question named in an abstract noun: duty, egoism, sympathy, vanity, conscience.
moves.hint: Name the moral quality at stake in one noun: duty, vanity, sympathy.

moves.name: The qualified period
moves.does: A long sentence that corrects and qualifies itself as it goes.
moves.hint: Write a long sentence that corrects itself as it goes: “…, or rather …”, “…, though …”.

parts.says: Begins with the time, and a kind of man found in it.
parts.quote: In the days when the spinning-wheels hummed busily in the farmhouses

parts.says: Explains why country people feared such men.
parts.quote: how was a man to be explained unless you at least knew somebody who knew his father and mother?

parts.says: Comes down to one weaver in one village.
parts.quote: such a linen-weaver, named Silas Marner

parts.says: Describes him as the village boys saw him.

shapes.work: the opening of The Mill on the Floss
shapes.cite: The Mill on the Floss, ch. 1

parts.says: Begins with the river and the plain, and no people.
parts.quote: A wide plain, where the broadening Floss hurries on

parts.says: Brings in an “I” who remembers the place.
parts.quote: I remember those large dipping willows

parts.says: Finds a little girl watching the mill.
parts.quote: That little girl is watching it too

parts.says: Wakes, and shows the scene was a dream of years ago.
parts.quote: Ah, my arms are really benumbed.

parts.says: Begins with a young wife crying alone.
Grants that such grief is common, and so is not pitied.
parts.quote: we do not expect people to be deeply moved by what is not unusual

parts.says: Claims there is tragedy in what is common.
parts.quote: That element of tragedy which lies in the very fact of frequency

parts.says: Says why we cannot bear to feel it.
parts.quote: it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel’s heart beat

parts.says: Ends on a hard word for all of us.

license.note: Published 1860–1876: public domain in the US.
